subject: community-medicine
title: Iceberg Phenomenon, Epidemiological Triad and Risk Factors

steps.title: The floating tip: clinical cases
steps.tx: The **iceberg phenomenon** compares disease in a community to an iceberg whose floating tip holds the clinical cases a physician actually sees. Those visible cases bring symptoms, seek care and enter records. Everything planners count in routine statistics comes from this small tip, which is why clinic experience alone misleads community diagnosis so reliably.
steps.say: Picture an iceberg. The small floating tip holds the clinical cases doctors see: patients with symptoms, who seek care and enter the records. Routine statistics describe only that tip, which is why clinic experience alone misleads community diagnosis.

steps.tx: What a physician sees, and what routine statistics count, is only the tip in the **iceberg phenomenon**. Those people have symptoms, they attend, and they are written into records. Latent infection, inapparent illness, presymptomatic disease, undiagnosed cases and carriers stay below the waterline and never correct the register. A picture of disease learned entirely from the ward therefore misstates the district. Community diagnosis has to look for the submerged mass, not only for the patients who found the clinic.
steps.say: The floating tip of the iceberg is the clinical cases doctors actually meet: symptomatic people who seek care and enter the notes. Routine statistics describe only that tip. Silent infection, early disease and carriers remain underwater, which is why ward experience alone gives a false community diagnosis.

vis.alt: An iceberg in cross section has clinical cases above the waterline and latent, inapparent, presymptomatic, undiagnosed and carrier states below it.
vis.caption: Only symptomatic clinical cases stand above the waterline, while hidden infection, early disease, undiagnosed illness and carriers form the submerged mass. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: The submerged mass below the waterline
steps.tx: The **submerged portion** hides latent, inapparent, presymptomatic and undiagnosed cases plus carriers in the community. The waterline separates apparent from inapparent disease. This hidden mass forms an undiagnosed reservoir that keeps transmission going after visible cases are treated, which is why case treatment alone so often fails to control endemic disease.
steps.say: Below the waterline lies the hidden mass: latent, inapparent, presymptomatic and undiagnosed cases, plus carriers. That reservoir keeps transmission alive after visible cases are treated. Case treatment alone therefore fails against endemic disease again and again.

steps.title: Diseases where the hidden part dominates
steps.tx: In **hypertension and diabetes**, with anaemia, malnutrition and mental illness, unknown morbidity far exceeds known morbidity. Most hypertensive adults in a typical survey are undetected, untreated or uncontrolled, the pattern teachers call the rule of halves. Detecting the submerged part demands screening surveys, since waiting for symptoms guarantees that complications announce the disease first.
steps.say: Some diseases hide most of their burden. Hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, malnutrition and mental illness carry far more unknown than known cases. Surveys find most hypertensive adults undetected or uncontrolled. Screening, not waiting for symptoms, exposes that hidden share.

rows: Mild cases never reach a clinic

steps.title: Spectrum of disease beside the iceberg
steps.tx: The **spectrum of disease** runs from subclinical infection at one end to fatal illness at the other, with mild to severe illness between, like colours shading along a band. Leprosy shows the full range, from indeterminate patches to lepromatous disease. Rabies breaks the pattern as an exception with almost uniform fatality once symptoms begin.
steps.say: A sister idea grades severity. Disease runs from silent infection through mild and severe illness to death, shading like colours on a band. Leprosy displays the full range. Rabies breaks the pattern, killing almost uniformly once symptoms begin.

steps.tx: The **spectrum of disease** is a graded band, not a single picture: subclinical infection, then mild, moderate and severe illness, then death. Leprosy occupies the whole band, from an indeterminate patch to lepromatous disease. Rabies is the exception used in teaching because, once symptoms have started, fatality is almost uniform and there is no mild surviving form to place beside the fatal end. Naming a disease without saying where on the band the patient sits hides that range.
steps.say: Disease severity shades from silent infection through mild and severe illness to death. Leprosy shows every step, from indeterminate patches to lepromatous disease. Rabies does not shade: after symptoms begin it kills almost every patient, so it is the exception to a graded spectrum.

vis.alt: A severity band runs from subclinical infection through mild, moderate and severe illness to fatal disease, with forms of leprosy marked along the band.
vis.caption: Severity is drawn as a continuous band from silent infection to death, and leprosy is marked from indeterminate patches through to lepromatous disease. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: The epidemiological triad
steps.tx: The **epidemiological triad** explains disease through agent, host and environment in interaction. Mere presence of all three starts nothing; disease begins when they interact in the prepathogenesis phase. Their combination also sets the distribution of disease, from a single case to an epidemic, which makes the triad the first diagram to draw in any outbreak answer.
steps.say: Three corners explain occurrence. Agent, host and environment must interact; mere presence starts nothing. Their combination also decides whether one case or an epidemic follows. Draw this triangle first in any outbreak answer.

rows: Who gets it and why them?
Where and when does transmission favour?

steps.title: Agent, host and environment factors
steps.tx: **Agent factors** span biological agents, nutrients in excess or deficiency, physical agents such as heat and radiation, chemical agents, mechanical agents and social agents. Host factors are intrinsic: age, sex, heredity, immunity and behaviour. Environmental factors are extrinsic and split into physical, biological and psychosocial surroundings that favour or block the meeting.
steps.say: Fill each corner. Agents include microbes, nutrients, heat, chemicals, mechanical forces and social agents. Host factors stay intrinsic: age, sex, heredity, immunity, behaviour. Environment stays extrinsic, split into physical, biological and psychosocial surroundings.

rows: Biological, nutrient, physical, chemical, mechanical, social

steps.title: Risk factors: causative, contributory, predictive
steps.tx: A **risk factor** may be truly causative, like smoking for lung cancer; merely contributory, like inactivity for coronary disease; or predictive only in a statistical sense, like illiteracy for perinatal mortality. Detection should trigger one question: can this factor be reduced cheaply, and will reducing it delay the outcome? Otherwise measurement wastes resources.
steps.say: Not every association causes disease. Smoking truly causes lung cancer. Inactivity contributes to coronary disease. Illiteracy only predicts perinatal deaths statistically. After detecting any factor, ask whether cutting it cheaply would delay the outcome.

steps.title: Modifiable versus unmodifiable risk
steps.tx: **Modifiable risk factors** such as smoking, hypertension, raised cholesterol, inactivity and obesity yield to intervention and guide individual care. Unmodifiable factors such as age, sex, race, family history and genetic make-up cannot change; they act as signals that alert services to likely outcomes. Prevention budgets belong mainly to the first group, screening logic to the second.
steps.say: Sort factors by whether action can change them. Smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol, inactivity and obesity yield to intervention. Age, sex and family history cannot change, so they serve as warning signals. Budgets follow the first group; screening follows the second.

steps.title: Risk groups and the risk approach
steps.tx: The **risk approach** identifies groups such as at-risk mothers, infants, families, chronically ill and elderly people by defined biological, physical and socio-cultural criteria, then directs action to them first. Its slogan runs: something for all, but more for those in need, in proportion to need. Scarce resources then reach the likeliest cases before the rest.
steps.say: Group level thinking completes the lesson. Defined criteria pick out at-risk mothers, infants, families and elderly people, and services reach them first. The slogan says it: something for all, more for those in need, in proportion to need.
